newsitem.title: USA: Amtrak, others back use of gas tax money for rail.
newsitem.headline: Amtrak, others back use of gas tax money for rail.

text.p: The proposed diversion to Amtrak of half-a-cent of the 4.3 cents per gallon federal gasoline tax was essential to keep the passenger line running, Amtrak's chairman told the Senate Finance Committee Wednesday.

Committee chairman Sen. William Roth, a Delaware Republican, and Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat and the panel's ranking minority member, have co-sponsored a bill proposing the half-cent tax for a rail trust fund.
Roth said the legislation would give Amtrak $4 billion over five years, providing the funds necessary to make capital improvements and to operate in a businesslike fashion.

Amtrak chairman Thomas Downs noted that Amtrak was already borrowing money to meet its payroll and needed several billion dollars in coming years to complete a modernization effort that included buying 18 high speed trains for its busy East Coast corridor.
"Amtrak is in difficult shape," he told the panel. "We cannot preserve a national passenger rail system through yet another year of inadequate funding."
Downs's assessment was backed by testimony from passenger, environmental and labor union groups.

Phyllis Scheinberg, a railroad specialist at the General Accounting Office, the investigative unit of Congress, said Amtrak's goal of operating self-sufficiency by 2002 was heavily dependent on dedicated funding, such as the half-cent gas money.

But the future of the legislation was uncertain, according to Congressional aides. They said the billions of dollars diverted from the 4.3 cents a gallon tax would reduce the money that went into federal deficit reduction, the aim of the tax when it was passed in 1993.

And the powerful chairman of the House Transportation, Science and Infrastructure Committee, Bud Shuster, has argued that if half a cent is used for Amtrak, the rest of the 4.3 cents levied on gas should be spent on highways.
An aide to Shuster, a Pennsylvania Repubican, said that money has not been the problem at Amtrak, but a corporate structure written into the law creating Amtrak, has been.
He said there needed to be reforms to allow Amtrak to reduce some of its expensive severance pay requirements, to contract out work and to close or reduce service on unprofitable routes.
